I said I'll pay you, I'd like to know what you charge. He…

232.t: Ordered out of town in fifteen minutes
232.s: A white man gives the band fifteen minutes to leave; Melvin has them push the bus down the road.

Directly, a white guy came up, Little Dick was sitting behind the steering wheel, he hit…

232.s: Lead trumpeter Embray is pushed off the sidewalk and white band manager Iller has trouble riding to the Black hotel and the Esquire Club.

So when he met this officer--this is in Miami--when he met this officer, he didn't…

86.t: Beatings and injuries: Lucky Millinder, Pete Prince and Archie Hall
86.s: He tells of violence against musicians, including Pete Prince's mouth injury and the Jim Europe band's Archie Hall.
86.q: Some of them…when you were born in the South, you know what to expect. Born in the North, naturally you’ll go down there and do something stupid not even knowing that you’re wrong, ‘cause who’s who to say who’s right and who’s wrong. Who are they to say you can’t go in this place, you can’t do…

86.s: The band all carried guns for protection but never used them.
86.q: On the Southern tours. Just for protection. But we were jeopardizing our own lives when we did that because there is a whole town, a whole police force against you down there.

86.s: Police led the band out of town, and Jimmy Rushing was forced to remove his white socks.
86.q: Oh yeah, one time the police led us out of town, and told us not to come back. We were late playing on a job in Bunkie, Louisiana. And because the bus broke down, we had no choice but to get there late. So, Jimmy Rushing, well he used to sit in front of the bandstand and he used to wear white socks…

406.t: Touring the South: Jimmy Rushing's white socks and the Chattanooga cop
406.s: Only Cab and Duke could afford Pullmans. With Moten in Beaumont a man made Jimmy Rushing remove white socks at gunpoint. In Chattanooga a friendly Irish cop let Barefield walk at night.
406.q: Well, I went down there with Benny Moten's band. We traveled all through -- in fact, that was our stomping ground, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas, Little Rock, Arkansas, and I went down there with Fletcher, and, well, you know, you just know where to go and where to stay.

406.t: Refused service in Kankakee and other Illinois incidents
406.s: In 1930 he and banjoist Mike McKendrick were refused lunch at a bus stop in Kankakee, and a cook came out with a cleaver. With the Virginia Ravens they could play dances but not eat or sleep in some Illinois towns.
406.q: expect because in the year earlier we had eaten in a -- many a kitchen, back up in a restaurant and also taken food out, and in fact, one time we was coming with Bernie Young's band and had gone down to Tulsa, Oklahoma. We -- some of the guys came back in cars, and Mike McKendrick -- I don't know…

406.t: Segregation in Florida and violence against musicians
406.s: He tells of Florida in the Ella period, where Buddy Rich was beaten for listening to Lucky Millinder and the Whispering Band of Gold was beaten by police.
406.q: Well, in fact, in Florida you couldn't even play for a white dance in Florida. I remember when I was there with Ella, when I went to Florida, Chauncey Horton drew $50.00, he sent home and went down to the telegraph station. I get a call to come down there and rescue him because he had too much…

166.t: Arrested at the train station: the commissary waitress, the reserved seat and the police c

166.ch: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
166.q: Yeah. Boy, that was a beautiful group. One of the best feelings I've had in a long time on a bandstand. One of the few, you know. Where you'd look forward to getting to work. Couldn't get to work fast enough, you know. Because every night someone was inventing something new and they were falling…

166.s: Three men at the bar ask whether he'd rather be called 'Nigger' or 'darky'; he declines to fight and goes back to Bellson's.
166.ch: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York

455.s: Singer Arthur Lee Simpkins tried to protect a banker's son whom waiters beat after he called out a slur, so Earl bypassed Augusta.

18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road

119.t: Civil rights era riots on tour

450.t: Racism on tour: Philadelphia police and Basie's warning about Texas
450.s: Dave Lambert protected Jon Hendricks from Philadelphia police, and Basie warned them about playing a boxing ring in Texas.
450.q: Only in the City of Brotherly Love. And Dave Lambert saved Jon because the police there were very heavy at the time. 225.t: Racial conditions touring, and the St. Louis incident
225.s: Johnson recalls mostly psychological rather than physical violence and cannot recall a St. Louis attack.
225.ch: Jazz at the Philharmonic and Count Basie
225.q: There were certainly incidents, and there were certain unpleasant occurrences, of course. But I haven’t held any in my memory bank as being outstanding. Just the norm.

88.t: The attack on Nat Cole on stage in Birmingham
88.s: Men rushed the stage and one hit Nat before detectives pulled him off; the next morning over 100 white people apologized at the airport.

66.t: Menace in Memphis: lynching threats, the streetcar and the kidnap plot
66.s: At a club outside Memphis she was threatened as a Northerner. She worked for Mrs. Singleton, was frightened on a streetcar, and had to leave when a Mississippi farmer paid the cook to kidnap her.
66.ch: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City

Before John got his combo I got a little job out on the outskirts of Memphis and these people were ringing a bell and saying, "I want this," and telling me,…

And they came in and at the time, she was sitting in the seat, and Louis -- she was telling Louis something, Louis was on the edge of the arm of the bus, that's what it was, the arm of the seat, when the guys came in. I said, "what you mean you can't put me on there?" "Because that's a drawing room". I said, "yes I bought that. I got it". So…

94.t: The Dothan hotel, a burned mattress, and the bellboy years later
94.s: Staying in a white hotel as an Indian, Moore burned a mattress, left quietly, and was asked about it by the bellboy when he played Dothan with Armstrong.
94.q: There was one time, we were playing Dothan, Alabama, and there's no black hotel in Dothan so everyone is staying at private homes that take care of the musicians except that one guy, Foots. Foots didn't have a room at all, he couldn't find a vacant room anywhere so I gave up my room and gave my…

238.s: The incident made her decide she would not spend her life that way; she says Lake Charles itself had no such trouble.
238.ch: Life on the road in the South
238.q: Well, offhand, that was the one that really stood out in my mind all these many, many years, because it was a frightening experience. I personally don't think that they would have harmed me.
